And like the Bar-boy I When you bring ready mony, and keepe touch All's pay'd ſir, and y'are welcome. All thoſe croſſes that I have figur'd on the Princes Coyne, ſtand ſtill betwixt me and danger,
NOw we have paſſ'd our more retired houres To holy uſes as our vowes compell; In zealous and Religious exerciſes, In Viſitation of the weake and ſicke, To ſtrengthen thoſe that ſtagger with our prayers, And ghoſtly counſell; now night calls us home Unto our Cloyſter, there to ſpend the reſt Of our late houres in thoughts contemplative, And ſacred Meditations. Mercy Heaven how ſwift time runs? Thou ſay'ſt true, how ſhall we ſpend the night then? Knocke good Frier Iohn, and begge us a nights lodging. But Devotion ſhould alwayes wake; Where's the good man your Husband? 'Tis no vaine pleaſure, Or evill purpoſe that hath kept us out, But Chriſtian zeale to viſite and confirme Them, for his ſake to whom our lives are vow'd; Grant us reliefe and harbour. My good Dame, You ſee me aged, and farre ſpent in yeares, Decrepit, and unfit for dalliance, And ſhould my youthfull Novice ſtrive t' exceed His Lawfull bounds, I am neere to counſell him, But he was never guilty of ſuch thoughts. Then grant us the leaſt ſhelter, any place, By or remote, to keepe us from the cold; Stable, or Barne, if you be ſo provided, Or any out Roome where's but hay, or ſtraw To wrap us in till Morning. Grant us this, and you ſhall have the aſſiſtance of our prayers In all our Trentalls, Maſſes, Dirges, Oriſons, Your ſoule ſhall be remembred; but if we Should by your rude remorceleſſe cruelty Miſcarry in our perſons, in this raw And ſo bleake cold; the price of our two lives Muſt be of you exacted. Gentle Dame, for reverence of my yeares and gravity, And for my Covents Order; for my Name And my profeſſion, grant Frier Bernard this Harbour from Froſt and Snow. Now Heavens Beniſon fall on thy head, that two Religious men art ſo obſequious; gentle Novice, be Civill and much obſervant, 'tis a courteſie We ſcarce can find elſe where. All neceſſities are ever to bee pardon'd, once, like Horſes, Let's lodge in our owne Litter; I commend The womans modeſty, that is ſo curious, Her Husband being from home, to avoyd ſcandall, And mens baſe imputations. We entertaine it gladly, And thanke you my good Dame, I am for ſleepe, That's this my nights ambition. Exceſſe, my Hoſt, can purchaſe no excuſe, But modeſt mirth, tranſgreſſing not his true And lawfull bounds, is good and commendable; Now give us leave to bid you welcome home. By Art, can that be done? Oh prophane, and fearefull! Art Magicke! didſt thou ever ſtudy that? It is againſt our Order. What doth my Novice meane? Not poſſible in Art. How comes this? 'Tis above wonder. Tell me, Frier Iohn ? This to me appeares beyond imagination, Nay, gentle Hoſteſſe ſit. But how came this? Rather good morrow. Give me but leave to take my ſecond eyes, I will reſolve you preſently. Horrible; what tremour this begets? So this Indenture ſpeakes. In theſe conditions, I like a cunning Lawyer find a Clauſe to cheate the Divell, and to ſave a ſoule; Be'ſt thou the greateſt fell with Lucifer, Nay he himſelfe, I now am arm'd for thee: what claim'ſt Thou of this man? Which is not forfeit. By helpe of Heaven I ſhall: this deede thus runs; When all his Creditors are ſatisfied, His Bonds diſcharg'd and cancell'd, debts full paid, His Morgages call'd in, his words redeem'd, This Bond is then in vertue; not till then. Yes, but againſt the Divell. What were the ſummes for which he ſtood ingag'd? Both are quit, As thou thy ſelfe ſhalt to thy griefe confeſſe; For I will prove him more indebted now Than e're he was before. To thee, Whom till he have diſcharg'd the utmoſt penny, The Bond's of no effect. I am inform'd to th'full; if this be true, Divell, th' art honeſt, and ſhalt have thy due: Aſſociate me Frier Iohn.
Holy Father, I am affraid time hath prevented us, 'Tis now paſt Eight, and, but I much miſtake, I heard the warning of the Cloyſter Bell, Which tells us, if we reach not inſtantly W'are for this night excluded. W'are now at Iſlington, What hope have we to get to Crutched Friers Before the Gates be ſhut, and the Keyes carried Up to the Abbots Chamber? We'le knocke here At the next ſigne, the good man I know well, Of honeſt converſation, of good life, And yet a boone companion; one that loves Good company, and to be merry with them. He, if he be at home, will bid us welcome: My Hoſteſſe too, a ſweet and ſmooth-fac'd wench, Courteous and kind, and wondrous well belov'd Of all her Neighbours; liberall to the Church, And much commended for her Charity. Let us not bauke her houſe. For Charity thoſe that would be admitted. Frier Bernard, and Frier Iohn. 'Las my kind Dame, not I. Can you be ſo hard-hearted unto men Of our ſo knowne Devotion? My holy Father, I know it well; I am preſcrib'd my limits, Which I am willing with all zeale t'obſerve; I would we knew our Lodging. So doe I, 'Tis one of our beſt Dames; but ſee, ſhe comes To give us entertainement Enter the Woman. At your beſt pleaſure. Exeunt. Frier Bernard's faſt, he ſnores and ſleepes as Snug as any Pigge in Peaſe-ſtraw; but my ſelfe Cannot once cloſe an eye, which makes me wonder That I am growe ſo wakefull. Dreame I? or i'ſt ſubſtantiall that I ſee? Was this your cunning Dame, to locke us up Like Priſoners, and afford us nought but ſtraw To feather our neſts withall? not allow us drinke, Food, nor a Candle, leaſt we ſhould fire the Houſe, For that is her excuſe; fire on you both, Have you theſe trickes? yet God a mercy cranny That I can ſpy all this. She brings in the Pullet. Doe you ſtraine curteſies? had I it in fingering I'de make you both make but a Fridayes feaſt; Oh how the ſteame perfumes my Noſtrils. I by my faith, for one that could come by't. That's my Qu. The worſe lucke; and yet I ſmell a ſupper. Say you ſo? Ile try what I can doe. Bid my Dame provide Cloath, Salt, and Trenchers. For ſuch proviſion truſt to my Art. Yes, by Art Magicke. But not as I will order it, feare it not. For a Supper, or ſo, but never durſt deale further; Will you furniſh a Table fit for meate? All voſtro comando, Aſt • rothe, il pane in h • c camera preſto. Oh, now 'tis done; mine Hoſt, put but your hand Into that Corner and pull forth two Loaves. But ſee what Art can doe. My Spirit whiſpers Orleance Grape's the beſt, What ſayes mine Hoſt to a pure Cup of Orleance? Ie vou pre Monſieur Aſterothe, once more A Cup of Divine Claret; no, a Bottle of ſome two quarts ▪ Gramercy, thou haſt done't, mine Hoſt, but caſt your eye Upon that place, and you ſhall find it there. But taſte mine Hoſt, and try if it be right. No hurt to you ſtill, Father. Let me ſee, there is a Midnight ſupper now ſerved in At Prague in Germany, where the Emperours Court Lyes for the moſt part, and ſeldome is he abſent; Among all all other dainties, ſpeake, what diſh Deſire you from the Table? What ſay you to a Pullet piping hot, Now ſtanding on the Dreſſer? But once more Ile employ thee, Aſterothe, For this night no more trouble thee. Veni, aſſiſte, & in hac re ſuccurre ; I ſmell the Pullet Smoaking, and Sauce unto't. Somewhere about this Roome, who hath the Key Of that ſame Cupboord? Call for it, good mine Hoſt, You ſee I come neere nothing, uſe faire play, Saw neither fire nor candle to provide this, Toucht neither Locke nor Key within your houſe, But was aſleepe i'th'ſtraw; unlocke mine Hoſt, See what the Cupboord yeelds. What finde you there? You ſee what Art can doe. Ile talke with you anon, in the meane time Eate while 'tis hot, 't hath come a pretty Iourney, And marvell 'tis not cold. Many provide good Cates that taſt them not, Now bleſſing on their hearts. Aeſtroth, did you not heare me name him? One of the foure great Spirits, that have Dominion O're the foure quarters of the Earth: good Dame, Me thinkes you doe not eate. In what ſhape? Oh 'tis too terrible, it would fright us all. What, in his terrors? he would make you mad, Diſtracted and amaz'd, yet, good mine Hoſt, To give you all content, I could be willing To ſhew him but in ſome familiar ſhape, Such as ſhould not affright you. Have you no Neighbour whom you beſt affect, whoſe Shape he might aſſume t'appeare leſſe terrible? Soft, let me pauſe; It muſt be ſome that ſtill wake at theſe houres, We have no power o're ſleepers; ſay I bring him In perſon of ſome Watchman? Or in the habit of your Conſtable? Why then his. But mine Hoſt, reſolve me one thing; ſhould great Aſterothe appeare to you in your Goſſips ſhape, How would you deale with him? No ſuch thing; you muſt imagine him what he appeares, An evill ſpirit, to kicke him, and defie him, As you would doe the Divell, otherwiſe When you are late abroad, and we gone hence, He'le haunt your houſe hereafter. I muſt tell you, 'tis meerely for your owne good, Appeare Aſteroth, Aſteroth appeare from underneath the bed In ſhape of Maſter Conſtable; do't when I ſay't, Not yet? Excruciabo te Aſteroth, in jam jam jam apparebis. Now mine Hoſt, either with zeale expell the Divell hence, Or have your houſe ſtill haunted. Ile tell you by the way; no queſtions now: Now good mine Hoſt we ſee the night quite ſpent And the bright day ſtarre riſing in the Eaſt ; We'le take our leaves; make much of our good Dame, And thinke no worſe of your good Officer, Your Goſſip and your Neighbour, in whoſe forme Aſteroth ſo late appear'd. Onely commend us to my Dame your wife, And thanke her for our Lodging. Exeunt Haile Gentlemen, this man that ſtands at Livery And ſaith he doth belong to a great Lord. Hath partly by intreates, part by command, Enforc'd me from my meditations backe To know his Lordſhips pleaſure. Expect you ſuch things from religious men, And of our holy Order? Now mercy Heaven who hath ſeduc'd you thus? Either I muſt take upon my ſelfe, and by ſome tricke evade it, Or elſe ſhame that which I have done before. What, you make me a Conjurer? Well, what's the buſineſſe? My good Maſter. As how? Lodge where the foule fiend walkes? A propper jeſt t'expoſe me to ſuch danger, So I might come to juſtifie the Proverbe, Where had the Divell the Frier, but where he was; But I muſt face it out: Pray Gentlemen, which of you all Hath ſeene that Viſion? in what ſhape walkes it? And I to heare't. What a ſhee Divell now? for all the World I would not once affront her; bring me hither Ten thouſand male Fiends, I could charme their tongues Before one Female fury. Had it bin great Belioth, Aſteroth, or Belzebub, I durſt affront them, and confront them too, Oh but the Divells Dam; why againſt her There is no Prayer, no Spell, no Exorciſme; No Circle that can hold her: But appear'd ſhe Wrinckled in Brow or faire and beautifull? So much the worſe, Well wot you that our Order is by Oath Confin'd from any meeting with that Sex, Eſpecially at Midnight; and ſo late; Scarce in the day-time durſt I meet a face Of ſuch Temptation, but in dead of reſt 'Twould ſcandalize my Order. Heavens Beniſon and mine light on you till I meet you next; But to lye there where a ſhe Divell haunts, (Leſſe with my Hoſtes by at Iſlington ) May the Grand Divell fetch me, bleſſe you all. Exit. Is that the Divell? Ten thouſand Creeds, as many Pater-noſters, Ave Maries ſtand betweene me and harme. 'Tis a plaine caſe. The Divell hath bragg'd he hath caught many a Frier, Now one hath caught the Divell. Yes, till thou pay'ſt him all his money downe, Which when thou doeſt th'art worthy to be damn'd. With all my heart, If this be Asteroth I ſo late invoakt, I never ſhall deſire His company, but on an empty ſtomacke. Ex. Friers.
Who's that abroad ſo late? Charity ſhould be in bed at Mid-night. Hee's gone from home, and that's a reaſon too We ſhut up doores thus early; ſay, what are you? Religious men, and keepe unlawfull houres? 'Twere ſuſpitious for me, but a lone woman, he abroad, To entertaine men of your ranke and place, VVhoſe luſts have all bin queſtion'd, and have drawne Good women of beſt rumour and report, Into foule ſcandall; therefore pardon me, This night you get no entrance. Good, excuſe mee. Curſe upon them, No night but this to trouble me in? being ingaged To better fare by appointment. VVell Frier, you ſhall, But this provided, I will locke you up In a cloſe Garret, and my ſelfe keepe the Key To avoid ſuſpition; you ſhall have freſh ſtraw, But other Bedding none, no fire nor Candle, Beere, Ale, nor any ſuch commodity, Now in my Husbands abſence; ſo, pray enter, And this I doe for Charity. I have onely a Cock-loft, pleaſe you gentle Friers, To make beſt uſe of that and ſome freſh ſtraw, Beſt harbour that my Husbands abſence yeelds Y'are welcome to. Pleaſe you enter, but yet no further then Ile locke you in Ile keepe the Key my ſelfe. Whoſe there? Not Maſter Conſtable? Have you diſpoſ'd your Watch? Not too loud, meane time I ſoftly will ſneake downe The Staires, and ſoftly let you in. I was in feare you would have broke with me, But now I ſee y'are currant. Piping hot, Ile goe fetch Salt and Trenchers. Now let's be merry, but in any caſe Speake not too loud, leaſt we ſhould wake the Friers. Two Abbey Lubbers that are lockt up faſt, Of whom I could not rid me; but I thinke I have fitted them, they have neither light nor bed, Nor any other Comfort. Doe you't, I am no Carver. If I begin, may I ne're eate more. If that ſhould be my Husband? You were ſham'd, I quite undone; he knockes againe; Upon my life 'tis he. My Husbands voice, who's there? Creepe beneath the Bed. Now to convey theſe victuals hence, and put out the fire, Lord Husband is it you? who lookt for you ſo late? Theſe ſhall into the Cupboord, if the ſmell Betray's not w'are ſafe. I am comming, good lye cloſe, and if I can get him Once to bed, I have a tricke to ſhift you. Lord Husband that you'le venter whom ſo late, So many Knaves abroad? What, talke of Victuals now? is this a time of night? Had I knowne But of your comming home I had provided, But now I pray to bed, this cold ſo troubles me. You ſee the fire's quite out. Would houſe and all were fir'd, So ſome of us were out on't. No hurt man; nay, pray will you to bed? Two Friers ſhut from their Covents, wanting harbour, Begg'd lodging with ſuch importunity They would not be deny'd; at length I pittied them, And yet to make them ſure, I lockt them faſt Up in the Straw-loft, and ſee, here's the Key, Th'are faſt enough for ſtarting. Frier Bernard, and Frier Iohn. Call them up? what time ſhall we to bed then? To your bellies pots and all. Not ſo much as a cantell of Cheeſe, or cruſt of bread, That can this night be come by (for your throates, Ile rather ſee you choakt.) What a leering eye the Frier caſt towards the Cupbord? We ſhall have now ſome fooling. You ſee to pleaſe you, we can doe any thing. Pox on the Frier, have you theſe trickes? Your Divells take you; you know where's the beſt liquor. The Divell take all ſuch ſmell-feaſts. A poyſon on thee, would it might prove ſo to thee, It was never provided for thoſe chopps. But curſe on thine, and on thy ſtomacke too. I could eate thee. More ſcurvy trickes Frier Iohn, I may live to cry quit tance with you. Ile after him ▪ and leaſt he ſhould beare downe part Of the houſe, Ile let him out of doores. For reverence of your Order.
My Watch is ſet, charge given, and all at peace, But by the burning of the Candle blew, Which I by chance eſpyed through the Lanthorne, And by the dropping of the Beadles Noſe, I ſmell a Froſt; now to prevent this cold, To which I am ſubject, I have made my Deputy, Given up my ſtaffe and power into his hands; My ſelfe intending to ſpend all this night Here, at an honeſt Neighbours; ſome proviſion I have ſent in, and ſome I have brought along, A caſt of Manchets, and a Bottle to Of the beſt Wine in Turnball, which, they ſay All London cannot better: Silent all, None ſtirring neere, Ile knocke but ſoftly for feare Of waking Neighbours. 'Tis I. The ſame faire love. Yes, at you further Corner. Gramercy wench; the kindeſt loving Neighbour the Towne yeelds, the Hamlet cannot match her; a ſmug Laſſe, And one that knowes it too; I would not looſe her For halfe my ſtate in the Pariſh, while I'me in Office, She's ſafe as Mouſe in Mill: Oh, are you come? Sweet a kiſſe, and harke in thine eare. Frier Iohn peepes out above. Here's to thy good fat Pullet that's within, Two fine Cheat Loaves were ſent me from the Court, A Cup of Nipſitate briske and neate; The Drawers call it Tickle-braine, 'twill do't, But is the Roaſt-meat ready? Quicke, good Wench. The Friers? what Friers? Tuſh, no matter, What's that to us? Come ſweet, cut up the Pullet, And after we'le to Bed. In faith it ſhall be thine. Well, ſince you'le force me to't, I will make bold this once. One knocks at the doore. Ha, what then? What ſhall become of me? Doeſt thou not thinke he'le ſpare an Officer? But fall on the Kings Image? Where, which way? I, if my ſwell betray me not. I doe feele I had need of ſhift already.
Why Nan, aſleepe or dead? Why do'ſt not open doore? Why do'ſt not riſe? I'me almoſt ſtarved, prethee make haſt. I feare no robbing, and for my Carkaſſe, I ſtill beare About me to defend that, I've travell'd hard to day, And am very hungry prethee wife ſee what thou haſt in the houſe? Talke not to me, ſomething I muſt and will have. Cold troubles me, lay me ſome Faggots on. Ile have't reviv'd. Now bleſſe us wife, what noiſe is in the Garret? Thankes good Frier Bernard, Now as I live, would I had ſome good cheere, No better then I would pay for; but ſhe tells me There's nothing to be compaſſ'd. But any fare that would content the ſtomacke. But Frier Iohn, how ſhall we come by meate? Can Frier Iohn Conjure? Nan, when I ſay? Nor any heere? Would we might ſee them. Are you in earneſt? Two fine and delicate Manchets. I ſhall. Faith I ſay, would I might ſee't. Moſt admirable, ſee, here's a Bottle full. Excellent ſtuffe, I ne're dranke better Clarret. Any thing. Nothing better.
speeches.Wi. [Nan]: I have got ſuch a cold, a cough withall, I thought I ſhould have dyed; ſtay but a little Till I have caſt my Petticoate about me, Ile quickely let you in; the fire's quite out, No ſigne of any Feaſt. You're ſuch another man?
See how ſhe ſtirres? I would have had ſome company, I had not Such an appetite to be merry for an houre this ſeven yeare; That I could tell where to call up ſome good fellow That I knew, we would not part theſe two houres.
Bed me no bedds, Ile know the reaſon of't. Do'ſt thou know them? Frier Bernard, and Frier Iohn ? th'onely good Ladds That I deſir'd to meet with; I beſhrew thee They had no better welcome; goe, unlocke, Intreat them hither, we will have one cup To th'health of all their Covent. Time enough, early betimes, nay, quick Nan, Frier Iohn there? The bonnieſt Lad e're wore portace in a ſtring, Or mumbled Maſſe, or Mattins; I but wiſh'd And ſee, 'tis come to paſſe; the other to, Though he be ſtrict of life, yet will ſometimes Be merry, if he like his company; But my kind honeſt bald-pate, Frier Iacke, Enter woman and Friers. I ſhall be glad to ſee him; welcome faith, With reverence, Father, to your gravity, Be not offended if Frier Iohn and I Be, not exceeding compaſſe, a little merry, And play with the Pot; fill ſome in. Bread and Drinke? how ſhall we come by Meate? I, but where? Marry Nan, my Wife. A hot fat Pullet, newly dreſſ'd and ſauc'd. I never heard the like, Good wine, good bread, good victuals, ſtomacke good, And all to meete together? nay fall to, And he be thank'd that ſent it. I pray Frier Iohn, what ſpirit doe you deale with? And what's hee? Could you not ſhew your Divell for a need, To one that faine would ſee him? Why in his owne. Yet would I ſee him. With all my heart. Yes, twenty I could name. No ſhape better. Why hee's my honeſt Goſſip. Why as my friend, my Neighbour, and my Goſſip. Feare not that, If kickes and ſpurnes will drive the Divell hence, Ile helpe to ſend him packing. Will kickes do't? Let me alone to conjure him, pox on the Divell, He hath put me in a ſweat. Yes, doe good Nan ; I thinke Frier Iohn I have bumbaſted the Devill; thankes for our Supper, French wine, and Spaniſh Loaves, I never taſted meat That more contented me. Good night Frier Iohn, and holy Father Bernard.
You heare that newes of M. Slightals frenzy, and his un doing? Thou knoweſt he loves me; I was ſtill his friend, And friend with friend what cannot he performe? Make thy ſelfe mine, Ile croſſe thy Mothers workings, And foole that Lords attempts; onely be you of a more Temperate humour, and more ſtay'd, obſerving but what I Shall project for you, and doubt not my performance. Then enough. In the meane time't ſhall be my providence To have my houſe unhaunted; come my Lord, Leade you the way, my wife and I will follow. Remember Nan. Exeunt. He. Even the ſame. 'Tis the ſame, I know him by his roaring. Enter Slightall. This. There Shall I be plaine, my Lord? I crave your pardon, Wife, for your rage I am arm'd, yes, If thou could'ſt encounter with Fleſh-hookes, and with Fire-brands; for I tell thee I am practiſ'd in the Divell: but to you, my Lord, I paſſ'd my faith unto this Gentleman, Had it beene done to you I ne're had broke it.
Ha? The Larum's given; For at that watch word ſtill the rufling noyſe begins.
Did you call? The Divell Belzebub, whom thou ſo late ſo loud didſt invocate As if all habits, faſhions, and attires Were not with me familiar? I ſometimes Into a Lawyer can tranſforme my ſelfe To delay Cauſes; then to a Divine, To deviſe new Sects, Sciſmes, and Hereſies: To a Taylor for new faſhions: to a Sempſter, I was firſt Father for this yellow Sterch, Which did ſucceed the blew; to a Feather-maker For Gentlewomans Fans, mens ſpriggs, and falls; Sometimes I am a Page, and daily attend Upon my Lords luxurious appetites: Then can I play the Maſter, Knight, and Lord, And then coyne ſtrange varieties of riots, Luſts, and exceſſes, never heard before. Indeed, what can I not? It never was my ſtudy, and of all things I onely except that. Yes, both on ſoule and body, where I am ſuffered. How then came all thoſe Pulpit Hereſies That have with Chriſtians, Chriſtians ſet at odds? I read to that great Doctor Arius, That poyſon'd three parts of the Chriſtian World; There's not a Sectary, nor a Sciſmaticke, To whom I am not Tutor. No. Tuſh, that with eaſe I can. At pleaſure. Am I not Titled Prince of all the World? And lyes there that in this great Univerſe Excepted from my large Dominion? Am I not Mammon too, the god of gold, Soveraigne of all Exchequors, treaſures, mints, And thoſe rich Mines that ſet the World at odds? In ſearch of which men hazard dangerous Seas, Expoſe them to diſeaſes, and ſtrange Climates, Above their natures: Gold? I am Father of it, And have it in abundance. I will; but on condition. That when thy wiſhes have attain'd effect, Thou art full handled, haſt paid all thy debts, And nothing ow'ſt to any, I may then Moſt freely claime thy ſoule. Thy conſcience is a Thouſand, that ſhall ſerve; Let me but have't confirm'd beneath thy hand, And my Exchequor's open. Come, withdraw, we'le Have't confirm'd within. Exeunt. You are ſad ſir? No ſuch thing; the buſineſſe that I come to treat with thee Is of another nature. Have I not kept my word? Stor'd thee with all the ſuppliments Mans uſe can aske. Nay, was not I aſſiſtant in this quarrell, prompting thy Man to come to thy releaſe, juſt at the inſtant danger: Then ſpeake freely, Did'ſt ever in thy life time meete a friend, Whoſe word, aſſured truſt, and conſtancy Could ranke with mine in all things? Proofe of thy gratitude, or to be term'd unthankefull. Wilt thou in meere Requitall of ſo many, doe to me one faire Office? There's a houſe haunted with a ſhe ſpirit, one of my Servants, and Kitchin maides in Hell, employ'd by me For ſome knowne cauſes, who hath play'd ſuch prankes there No man's ſo bold dares lodge within the roome, This bed would I have thee to undertake. Still amiſſe; have not I power o're al my creatures there To limit and command them? art not thou One of our houſe by Indenture? though to them Shee appear'd gaſtly, horrid, and deform'd, To thee ſhe ſhall ſeeme faire and beautifull, No whit inferiour to that Graecian Queene, That launcht 1 • 000. Ships from Aulis Gulfe, And brought them to the fatall ſiege of Troy. And ſo confirme thee A Minyon to the mighty Belzebub, And great in our blacke Kingdome. Exeunt. Now. 'Tis vaniſht into Aire, whence it was form'd. Not poſſible, untill you meet in Hell; ſo neere Thy Fate, and cannot now the terrour of that place Coole thy hot courage? ſee the forfeiture, And here I doe arreſt thee. Canſt thou deny thy deed? Who ſhall doe't. If I can prove that all thy debts be paid Thou art my owne, was't not, and ſpeake thy conſcience, Our joynt condition? That Uſurer's one of thy maine Creditors, But when thou waſt ſo free to pay thy debts, thou ne're Dream'ſt of thy forfeit; propoſe to him thy queſtion. 'Tis confeſſ'd. Theſe are diſcharg'd, what refuge haſt thou now? Nay bring me unto all thy Creditors; Ile prove thy debts diſcharg'd. But I muſt have my bargaine. Haſt thou not ow'd to theſe? Reſolve me friends, as you are Gentlemen, In what knowne ſummes did this man ſtand ingag'd to Each of you? That's all Gentlemen—morow Doe but name the man, to whom thou canſt appeale. And to whom there? Then to theſe, to both, or either, freely take thy choice. Reade there, and tell me what thou think'ſt of that. In th'interim, what's the beſt newes in the pariſh? Yes. I claime a ſoule. Shew me reaſons why. All this I grant, and call to witneſſe none Save his owne Conſcience; art thou not at freedome, And cleare from all the world? Speake, how that? Some fifteene thouſand pounds, which I have pay'd, And now the man owes nothing; therefore duely I Claime both ſoule and body. To whom? And am I tripp'd? Nay then I ſee vainely we Divells ſtand againſt the Church, they have ſtill the upper hand, I yeeld me vanquiſh'd; in the meame time Frier read And conceale. Gives him another paper to reade. Yet for my love, For all the good thou haſt receiv'd by me, For all my coſt and charges, large expence, As I acquit thee truely, ſo thou freely Lend me thine eare. Preſume thou ſhalt. And enjoy her to: Doe thou but hazard as thou did'ſt before And doubt not, ſhe's thine owne. As a contracted Bride and Bed-fellow. None.
speeches.Wo. [Mistress Changeable]: Wondrouſly. Ten daies, no more, Part of that time that Slightall hath bin Mad, My daughter paſt her ſences. No, onely one by Chamber ſtands remote, And in that after Midnight there's a noiſe, That troubles the whole houſe of howlings, ſhrickes, Fire-workes and Crackers, as if the great ſquib-maker Were new come from beyond Sea. Onely my deſperate Husband, who, one night, Would be ſo fooliſh venturous as lodge there, But did returne ſo frighted, told ſuch wonders, Still fright me to remember. Heaven reſt her ſoule, my mother. A Divell ſir like me? Here's now my Husband, he can ſpeake it all. And now art found. Made me againe thy Mother, and this worke, Your ever patient and obedient wife. Sicke in her Chamber, where ſhe keepes her Bed, And dares not thence remove.
speeches.Chan: So I have heard; but this cannot be ſhe, For this had with her beauty ſo much terrour, So much affright and horrour in her lookes, Such a confuſed noyſe, with helliſh ſounds Able to drive the ſences retrograde; Turne reaſon into madneſſe, and invert Capacity to fury; that, I vow I would not to be heire of all the World Endure like night againe. Enter Geffrey & Frier Iohn.
Conſcience? what in that is wanting he ſhall find Made good in Law.
speeches.Sl: Thoſe, my good ſword, this Booke, and my bold heart Are Guards ſufficient 'gainſt a thouſand ſhadowes Of no Corporeall eſſence capable. And I will, I bid thee that thy money Ne're ſhall doe, ſave thee.
speeches.Di: I am content, 'tis done; how ere thy ſoule I'me confident is won. Exeunt.
